nodes.name: Principal assertion of the spectral theorem
nodes.statement: The principal assertion of the spectral theorem is that every bounded normal operator $T$ on a Hilbert space induces (in a canonical way) a resolution $E$ of the identity on the Borel subsets of its spectrum $\sigma(T)$ and that $T$ can be reconstructed from $E$ by an integral. A large part of the theory of normal operators depends on this fact.
nodes.statement_short: The spectral theorem: a bounded normal operator induces a resolution of the identity on its spectrum and is recovered from it by integration.

nodes.name: Riesz representation theorem (complex Riesz-Markov-Kakutani)
nodes.statement: \fbox{\parbox{\linewidth}{ If $X$ is a locally compact Hausdorff space, then every bounded linear functional $\Phi$ on $C_0(X)$ is represented by a unique regular complex Borel measure $\mu$, in the sense that \begin{equation*} \Phi f = \int_X f \, d\mu \end{equation*} for every $f \in C_0(X)$. Moreover, the norm of $\Phi$ is the total variation of $\mu$: \begin{equation*} \|\Phi\| = |\mu|(X). \end{equation*}
nodes.origin_citation: Rudin, Real and Complex Analysis, Thm 6.19
assumptions: $X$ is a locally compact Hausdorff space
conclusions: every bounded linear functional $\Phi$ on $C_0(X)$ is represented by a unique regular complex Borel measure $\mu$, in the sense that \begin{equation*} \Phi f = \int_X f \, d\mu \end{equation*} for every $f \in C_0(X)$.
the norm of $\Phi$ is the total variation of $\mu$: \begin{equation*} \|\Phi\| = |\mu|(X). \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Every bounded functional on $C_0(X)$ is integration against a unique regular complex Borel measure, with norm equal to its total variation.

nodes.name: Variation of a vector-valued measure
nodes.statement: Let $(X, \mathcal{A})$ be a measurable space and let $Y$ be a Banach space. For a vector-valued measure $\mu: \mathcal{A} \to Y$, the \textbf{variation} of $\mu$ is the set function $|\mu|: \mathcal{A} \to [0, +\infty]$ defined by \begin{equation*} |\mu|(E) = \sup \left\{ \sum_{i=1}^n \|\mu(E_i)\|_Y : \{E_1, E_2, \ldots, E_n\} \text{ is a finite partition of } E \text{ in } \mathcal{A} \right\} \end{equation*} for each $E \in \mathcal{A}$.
differentia: \begin{equation*} |\mu|(E) = \sup \left\{ \sum_{i=1}^n \|\mu(E_i)\|_Y : \{E_1, E_2, \ldots, E_n\} \text{ is a finite partition of } E \text{ in } \mathcal{A} \right\} \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: The variation $|\mu|(E)$ is the sup over finite partitions of $E$ of the summed norms $\|\mu(E_i)\|_Y$.
nodes.label: def:variation

nodes.name: Equivalent form of the variation
nodes.statement: Equivalently, the above definition can be written as: \begin{equation*} |\mu|(E) = \sup \left\{ \sum_{i=1}^n \|\mu(E_i)\|_Y : E_i \in \mathcal{A}, \, E_i \cap E_j = \emptyset \text{ for } i \neq j, \, \bigcup_{i=1}^n E_i \subseteq E \right\} \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: The variation may equivalently be taken as a sup over finite disjoint families contained in $E$.

nodes.name: Proof of density of $C_c(X)$ in $L^p$
nodes.statement: Define $S$ as in Theorem 3.13. If $s \in S$ and $\varepsilon > 0$, there exists a $g \in C_c(X)$ such that $g(x) = s(x)$ except on a set of measure $< \varepsilon$, and $|g| \leq \|s\|_\infty$ (Lusin's theorem). Hence \begin{equation} \|g - s\|_p \leq 2\varepsilon^{1/p}\|s\|_\infty. \end{equation} Since $S$ is dense in $L^p(\mu)$, this completes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Approximate simple functions by $C_c$ functions via Lusin's theorem, then use density of simple functions.

nodes.name: Proof of Rudin 6.13
nodes.statement: By Theorem \ref{thm:polar_rep}, there is a function $h$, of absolute value 1, such that $d\lambda = h \, d|\lambda|$. By hypothesis, $d\lambda = g \, d\mu$. Hence \[ h \, d|\lambda| = g \, d\mu. \] This gives $d|\lambda| = \bar{h}g \, d\mu$. (Compare with Theorem 1.29.) Since $|\lambda| \geq 0$ and $\mu \geq 0$, it follows that $\bar{h}g \geq 0$ a.e. $[\mu]$, so that $\bar{h}g = |g|$ a.e. $[\mu]$. \qed
nodes.statement_short: Apply the polar representation to $\lambda$ and compare densities to get $\bar h g = |g|$ a.e.

nodes.name: Duality of $L^p$ and $L^q$
nodes.statement: Suppose $1 \leq p < \infty$, $\mu$ is a $\sigma$-finite positive measure on $X$, and $\Phi$ is a bounded linear functional on $L^p(\mu)$. Then there is a unique $g \in L^q(\mu)$, where $q$ is the exponent conjugate to $p$, such that \begin{equation} \Phi(f) = \int_X fg \, d\mu \quad (f \in L^p(\mu)). \end{equation} Moreover, if $\Phi$ and $g$ are related as in (1), we have \begin{equation} \|\Phi\| = \|g\|_q. \end{equation} In other words, $L^q(\mu)$ is isometrically isomorphic to the dual space of $L^p(\mu)$, under the stated conditions.

assumptions: $X$ be a locally compact Hausdorff space

nodes.name: Proof of uniqueness of the Riesz measure
nodes.statement: Suppose $\mu$ is a regular complex Borel measure on $X$ and $\int f \, d\mu = 0$ for all $f \in C_0(X)$. By Theorem \ref{thm:polar_rep} there is a Borel function $h$, with $|h| = 1$, such that $d\mu = h \, d|\mu|$. For any sequence $\{f_n\}$ in $C_0(X)$ we then have \begin{equation} |\mu|(X) = \int_X (\bar{h} - f_n)h \, d|\mu| \leq \int_X |\bar{h} - f_n| \, d|\mu|, \tag{3} \end{equation} and since $C_c(X)$ is dense in $L^1(|\mu|)$ (Theorem \ref{thm:Cc_dense_Lp}), $\{f_n\}$ can be so chosen that the last expression in (3) tends to 0 as $n \to \infty$. Thus $|\mu|(X) = 0$, and $\mu = 0$. It is easy to see that the difference of two regular complex Borel measures on $X$ is regular. This shows that at most one $\mu$ corresponds to each $\Phi$.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to a measure annihilating $C_0(X)$; via the polar representation and density of $C_c$ in $L^1(|\mu|)$ get $|\mu|(X)=0$.

nodes.name: Estimate (3) for $|\mu|(X)$
nodes.statement: |\mu|(X) = \int_X (\bar{h} - f_n)h \, d|\mu| \leq \int_X |\bar{h} - f_n| \, d|\mu|, \tag{3}

nodes.name: Existence of a dominating positive linear functional
nodes.statement: Consider a given bounded linear functional $\Phi$ on $C_0(X)$. Assume $\|\Phi\| = 1$. (Update statement to be the general case.) We shall construct a positive linear functional $\Lambda$ on $C_c(X)$, such that \begin{equation} |\Phi(f)| \leq \Lambda(|f|) \leq \|f\| \quad (f \in C_c(X)), \tag{4} \end{equation} where $\|f\|$ denotes the supremum norm.
nodes.origin_citation: Rudin, Real and Complex Analysis, Thm 6.19 (proof)
assumptions: a given bounded linear functional $\Phi$ on $C_0(X)$
conclusions: We shall construct a positive linear functional $\Lambda$ on $C_c(X)$, such that \begin{equation} |\Phi(f)| \leq \Lambda(|f|) \leq \|f\| \quad (f \in C_c(X)), \tag{4} \end{equation} where $\|f\|$ denotes the supremum norm.
nodes.statement_short: A norm-one functional on $C_0(X)$ is dominated by a positive linear functional $\Lambda$ on $C_c(X)$ with $|\Phi(f)|\le\Lambda(|f|)\le\|f\|$.
nodes.label: lem:exists_pos_lin_func

nodes.name: Construction of the positive functional $\Lambda$
nodes.statement: Assume $\|\Phi\| = 1$, without loss of generality. So all depends on finding a positive linear functional $\Lambda$ that satisfies (4). If $f \in C_c^+(X)$ [the class of all nonnegative real members of $C_c(X)$], define \begin{equation} \Lambda f = \sup \{|\Phi(h)| : h \in C_c(X), |h| \leq f\}. \tag{9} \end{equation} Then $\Lambda f \geq 0$, $\Lambda$ satisfies (4), $0 \leq f_1 \leq f_2$ implies $\Lambda f_1 \leq \Lambda f_2$, and $\Lambda(cf) = c\Lambda f$ if $c$ is a positive constant. We have to show that \begin{equation} \Lambda(f + g) = \Lambda f + \Lambda g \quad (f \text{ and } g \in C_c^+(X)), \tag{10} \end{equation} and we then have to extend $\Lambda$ to a linear functional on $C_c(X)$. Fix $f$ and $g \in C_c^+(X)$. If $\varepsilon > 0$, there exist $h_1$ and $h_2 \in C_c(X)$ such that $|h_1| \leq f$, $|h_2| \leq g$, and \begin{equation} \Lambda f \leq |\Phi(h_1)| + \varepsilon, \quad \Lambda g \leq |\Phi(h_2)| + \varepsilon. \tag{11} \end{equation} There are complex numbers $\alpha_i$, $|\alpha_i| = 1$, so that $\alpha_i \Phi(h_i) = |\Phi(h_i)|$, $i = 1, 2$. Then \begin{align} \Lambda f + \Lambda g & \leq |\Phi(h_1)| + |\Phi(h_2)| + 2\varepsilon \\ & = \Phi(\alpha_1 h_1 + \alpha_2 h_2) + 2\varepsilon \\ & \leq \Lambda(|h_1| + |h_2|) + 2\varepsilon \\ & \leq \Lambda(f + g) + 2\varepsilon, \end{align} so that the inequality $\geq$ holds in (10). Next, choose $h \in C_c(X)$, subject only to the condition $|h| \leq f + g$, let $V = \{x : f(x) + g(x) > 0\}$, and define \begin{align} h_1(x) & = \frac{f(x)h(x)}{f(x) + g(x)}, \quad h_2(x) = \frac{g(x)h(x)}{f(x) + g(x)} \quad (x \in V), \tag{12} \\ h_1(x) & = h_2(x) = 0 \quad (x \notin V). \end{align} It is clear that $h_1$ is continuous at every point of $V$. If $x_0 \notin V$, then $h(x_0) = 0$; since $h$ is continuous and since $|h_1(x)| \leq |h(x)|$ for all $x \in X$, it follows that $x_0$ is a point of continuity of $h_1$. Thus $h_1 \in C_c(X)$, and the same holds for $h_2$. Since $h_1 + h_2 = h$ and $|h_1| \leq f$, $|h_2| \leq g$, we have \begin{equation} |\Phi(h)| = |\Phi(h_1) + \Phi(h_2)| \leq |\Phi(h_1)| + |\Phi(h_2)| \leq \Lambda f + \Lambda g. \end{equation} Hence $\Lambda(f + g) \leq \Lambda f + \Lambda g$, and we have proved (10). If $f$ is now a real function, $f \in C_c(X)$, then $2f^+ = |f| + f$, so that $f^+ \in C_c^+(X)$; likewise, $f^- \in C_c^+(X)$; and since $f = f^+ - f^-$, it is natural to define \begin{equation} \Lambda f = \Lambda f^+ - \Lambda f^- \quad (f \in C_c(X), f \text{ real}) \tag{13} \end{equation} and \begin{equation} \Lambda(u + iv) = \Lambda u + i\Lambda v. \tag{14} \end{equation} Simple algebraic manipulations, just like those which occur in the proof of Theorem 1.32, show now that our extended functional $\Lambda$ is linear on $C_c(X)$.
nodes.statement_short: Construction: define $\Lambda f$ as a sup over $|h|\le f$, prove additivity on $C_c^+$, extend to real and complex parts. The key step splits $h$ into $h_1+h_2$ proportionally to $f,g$.

nodes.name: Proof of existence of the Riesz measure
nodes.statement: Once we have the $\Lambda$ from Lemma~\ref{lem:exists_pos_lin_func}, we associate with it a positive Borel measure $\lambda$, as in Theorem 2.14. The conclusion of Theorem 2.14 shows that $\lambda$ is regular if $\lambda(X) < \infty$. Since \begin{equation} \lambda(X) = \sup \{\Lambda f : 0 \leq f \leq 1, f \in C_c(X)\} \end{equation} and since $|\Lambda f| \leq 1$ if $\|f\| \leq 1$, we see that actually $\lambda(X) \leq 1$. We also deduce from (4) that \begin{equation} |\Phi(f)| \leq \Lambda(|f|) = \int_X |f| \, d\lambda = \|f\|_1 \quad (f \in C_c(X)). \tag{5} \end{equation} The last norm refers to the space $L^1(\lambda)$. Thus $\Phi$ is a linear functional on $C_c(X)$ of norm at most 1, with respect to the $L^1(\lambda)$-norm on $C_c(X)$. There is a norm-preserving extension of $\Phi$ to a linear functional on $L^1(\lambda)$, and therefore Theorem \ref{thm:Lp_duality} (the case $p = 1$) gives a Borel function $g$, with $|g| \leq 1$, such that \begin{equation} \Phi(f) = \int_X fg \, d\lambda \quad (f \in C_c(X)). \tag{6} \end{equation} Each side of (6) is a continuous functional on $C_0(X)$, and $C_c(X)$ is dense in $C_0(X)$. Hence (6) holds for all $f \in C_0(X)$, and we obtain the representation (1) with $d\mu = g \, d\lambda$.
nodes.statement_short: Build $\lambda$ from $\Lambda$ (Riesz for positive functionals), bound $\Phi$ in $L^1(\lambda)$, apply $L^1$-$L^\infty$ duality and extend by density.

nodes.statement: |\Phi(f)| \leq \Lambda(|f|) = \int_X |f| \, d\lambda = \|f\|_1 \quad (f \in C_c(X)). \tag{5}

nodes.statement: \Phi(f) = \int_X fg \, d\lambda \quad (f \in C_c(X)). \tag{6}

nodes.name: Proof that the norm equals the total variation
nodes.statement: Since $\|\Phi\| = 1$, (6) shows that \begin{equation} \int_X |g| \, d\lambda \geq \sup \{|\Phi(f)| : f \in C_0(X), \|f\| \leq 1\} = 1. \tag{7} \end{equation} We also know that $\lambda(X) \leq 1$ and $|g| \leq 1$. These facts are compatible only if $\lambda(X) = 1$ and $|g| = 1$ a.e. $[\lambda]$. Thus $d|\mu| = |g| \, d\lambda = d\lambda$, by Theorem \ref{thm:abs_integral}, and \begin{equation} |\mu|(X) = \lambda(X) = 1 = \|\Phi\|, \tag{8} \end{equation} which proves (2).
nodes.statement_short: From (6), $\int|g|\,d\lambda\ge1$ with $\lambda(X)\le1,|g|\le1$ forces equality; then $d|\mu|=d\lambda$ by Rudin 6.13.

nodes.name: Lower bound (7)
nodes.statement: \int_X |g| \, d\lambda \geq \sup \{|\Phi(f)| : f \in C_0(X), \|f\| \leq 1\} = 1. \tag{7}

nodes.name: Chain (8)
nodes.statement: |\mu|(X) = \lambda(X) = 1 = \|\Phi\|, \tag{8}

nodes.name: Hilbert space $H$ and closed subspace $K$
nodes.statement: Let $H$ be a complex Hilbert space and $K$ be a closed subspace of $H$.

nodes.name: Orthogonal complement
nodes.statement: We denote $K^\perp$ the orthogonal complement of $K$ in $H$.

nodes.name: Orthogonal decomposition
nodes.statement: Any vector $x \in H$ can be written as $x = x_K + x_{K^\perp}$, where $x_K \in K, x_{K^\perp} \in K^\perp$.
conclusions: $x = x_K + x_{K^\perp}$, where $x_K \in K, x_{K^\perp} \in K^\perp$

nodes.name: Orthogonal projection
nodes.statement: The map $p(K) : x \to x_K$ is called the orthogonal projection to $K$.

nodes.name: Orthogonal projections are self-adjoint idempotents
nodes.statement: It holds that $p(K) = p(K)^2 = p(K)^*$.
nodes.label: lem:projection_projection

nodes.name: Proof that $p(K)$ is a self-adjoint idempotent
nodes.statement: The first equality follows by the uniqueness of the orthogonal decomposition. The second equality follows because $\langle y, p(K)x \rangle = \langle y, x_K\rangle = \langle y_K, x \rangle = \langle p(K)y, x\rangle$ by orthogonality.
nodes.statement_short: Idempotence from uniqueness of the orthogonal decomposition; self-adjointness from orthogonality.

nodes.name: Self-adjoint idempotents are orthogonal projections
nodes.statement: For $p \in \mathcal{B}(H)$ such that $p = p^2 = p^*$, there is a closed subspace $K$ such that $p = p(K)$.
conclusions: there is a closed subspace $K$ such that $p = p(K)$
nodes.label: lem:exists_subspace

nodes.name: Proof that self-adjoint idempotents are orthogonal projections
nodes.statement: By $p = p^2$, it is a projection. Let $K$ be the image of $p$. Note that $x = (p + (1-p))x = px + (1-p)x$ for any $x \in H$ and $\langle px, (1-p)x\rangle = \langle x, (p-p)x\rangle = 0$. So this gives the orthogonal decomposition.
nodes.statement_short: Take $K$ the image of $p$ and check $x = px + (1-p)x$ is an orthogonal decomposition.

nodes.name: Convergence of orthogonal series (norm criterion)
nodes.statement: Let $\{x_n\}$ be a sequence of pairwise orthogonal vectors in $H$. Then the following are equivalent. \begin{itemize} \item $\sum_{n=1}^\infty x_n$ converges in the norm topology of $H$. \item $\sum_{n=1}^\infty \|x_n\|^2 < \infty$. \end{itemize}
assumptions: $\{x_n\}$ be a sequence of pairwise orthogonal vectors in $H$
conclusions: the following are equivalent. \begin{itemize} \item $\sum_{n=1}^\infty x_n$ converges in the norm topology of $H$. \item $\sum_{n=1}^\infty \|x_n\|^2 < \infty$. \end{itemize}
equivalent_conditions: $\sum_{n=1}^\infty x_n$ converges in the norm topology of $H$.
nodes.statement_short: An orthogonal series converges in norm iff the sum of squared norms is finite.
nodes.label: lem:sum_orthogonal

nodes.name: Proof of the norm criterion for orthogonal series
nodes.statement: Note that, by orthogonality, $\|\sum_{j=m}^n x_j\|^2 = \sum_{j=m}^n \|x_j\|^2$. Therefore, the second condition implies that the sequence $\sum_{j=1}^n x_j$ is Cauchy. Conversely, as $\sum_{j=1}^n x_j$ converges in norm, the square of its norm $\sum_{j=1}^n \|x_j\|^2$ converges.
nodes.statement_short: Pythagoras on partial sums gives the Cauchy criterion in both directions.

nodes.name: Convergence of orthogonal series (weak criterion)
nodes.statement: Let $\{x_n\}$ be a sequence of pairwise orthogonal vectors in $H$. Then the following are equivalent. \begin{itemize} \item $\sum_{n=1}^\infty x_n$ converges in the norm topology of $H$. \item $\sum_{n=1}^\infty \langle x, y\rangle$ converges for all $y \in H$. \end{itemize}
assumptions: $\{x_n\}$ be a sequence of pairwise orthogonal vectors in $H$
conclusions: the following are equivalent. \begin{itemize} \item $\sum_{n=1}^\infty x_n$ converges in the norm topology of $H$. \item $\sum_{n=1}^\infty \langle x, y\rangle$ converges for all $y \in H$. \end{itemize}
equivalent_conditions: $\sum_{n=1}^\infty x_n$ converges in the norm topology of $H$.
$\sum_{n=1}^\infty \langle x, y\rangle$ converges for all $y \in H$.
nodes.statement_short: An orthogonal series converges in norm iff it converges weakly against every $y$.
nodes.label: lem:sum_orthogonal'

nodes.name: Proof of the weak criterion for orthogonal series
nodes.statement: The first condition implies the second by Cauchy-Schwartz. Assume that $\sum_{n=1}^\infty \langle x, y\rangle$ converges for all $y \in H$. Define $\Lambda_n y = \sum_{j=1}^n \langle y, x_j\rangle$. As this converges for each $y$, by Banach-Steinhaus, $\{\|\Lambda_n\|\}$ is bounded. As $\|\Lambda_n\| = \sqrt{\sum_{j=1}^n \|x_j\|}$, this gives the first condition.
nodes.statement_short: Forward by Cauchy-Schwarz; converse by Banach-Steinhaus applied to partial-sum functionals $\Lambda_n$.

nodes.name: Resolution of the identity
nodes.statement: Let $\mathfrak{M}$ be a $\sigma$-algebra in a set $\Omega$, and let $H$ be a Hilbert space. For simplicity, we assume that $\Omega$ is a locally compact (Hausdorff) space. In this setting, a \emph{resolution of the identity} (on $\mathfrak{M}$) is a mapping \[ E: \mathfrak{M} \to \mathfrak{M}(H) \] with the following properties: \begin{enumerate} \item \( E(\emptyset) = 0\), \(E(\Omega) = I\). \item Each \( E(\omega) \) is a self-adjoint projection. \item \( E(\omega' \cap \omega'') = E(\omega')E(\omega'')\). \item If \( \omega' \cap \omega'' = \emptyset \), then \( E(\omega' \cup \omega'') = E(\omega') + E(\omega'') \). \item For every \( x \in H \) and \( y \in H \), the set function \( E_{x,y} \) defined by: \[ E_{x,y}(\omega) = (E(\omega)x, y) \] is a complex regular Borel measure on \( \mathcal{M} \). \end{enumerate}
differentia: Each \( E(\omega) \) is a self-adjoint projection.
For every \( x \in H \) and \( y \in H \), the set function \( E_{x,y} \) defined by: \[ E_{x,y}(\omega) = (E(\omega)x, y) \] is a complex regular Borel measure on \( \mathcal{M} \).
nodes.statement_short: A projection-valued map on a $\sigma$-algebra, multiplicative on intersections, finitely additive, with each $E_{x,y}$ a regular complex Borel measure.
nodes.label: def:resId

nodes.name: $E_{x,x}(\omega) = \|E(\omega)x\|^2$
nodes.statement: For any $x \in H$, \[ E_{x,x}(\omega) = (E(\omega)x, x) = \|E(\omega)x\|^2. \]
conclusions: \[ E_{x,x}(\omega) = (E(\omega)x, x) = \|E(\omega)x\|^2. \]
nodes.label: lem:resId_x_x

nodes.name: $E_{x,x}$ is a positive measure of mass $\|x\|^2$
nodes.statement: For any $x \in H$, \( E_{x,x} \) is a positive measure on \( \mathfrak{M} \) whose total variation is: \[ \|E_{x,x}\| = E_{x,x}(\Omega) = \|x\|^2. \]
conclusions: \( E_{x,x} \) is a positive measure on \( \mathfrak{M} \) whose total variation is: \[ \|E_{x,x}\| = E_{x,x}(\Omega) = \|x\|^2. \]
nodes.label: lem:resId_measure

nodes.name: The projections $E(\omega)$ commute
nodes.statement: For two $\omega_1, \omega_2$, \( E(\omega_1), E(\omega_2) \) commute.
conclusions: \( E(\omega_1), E(\omega_2) \) commute
nodes.label: lem:resId_comm

nodes.name: Proof that the projections commute
nodes.statement: By (\ref{itm:Rc}), any two of the projections \( E(\omega) \) commute with each other.
nodes.statement_short: Immediate from multiplicativity on intersections.

nodes.name: Disjoint sets give orthogonal ranges
nodes.statement: If \( \omega' \cap \omega'' = \emptyset \), then the ranges of \( E(\omega') \) and \( E(\omega'') \) are orthogonal to each other
conclusions: the ranges of \( E(\omega') \) and \( E(\omega'') \) are orthogonal to each other
nodes.label: lem:orthogonal_of_emptyset

nodes.name: Proof of orthogonality of ranges
nodes.statement: By (\ref{itm:Ra}), (\ref{itm:Rc}) and Theorem 12.14.
nodes.statement_short: From properties (a), (c) and Rudin's Theorem 12.14.

nodes.name: Finite additivity over disjoint families
nodes.statement: If $\{\omega_j\}$ is a finite family of mutually disjoint Borel sets, then $E(\bigcup_j \omega_j) = \sum_j E(\omega_j)$.
assumptions: $\{\omega_j\}$ is a finite family of mutually disjoint Borel sets
conclusions: $E(\bigcup_j \omega_j) = \sum_j E(\omega_j)$
nodes.label: lem:resId_iUnion

nodes.name: Proof of finite additivity
nodes.statement: By (\ref{itm:Rd}) and induction.
nodes.statement_short: Induction on the number of sets using property (d).

nodes.name: Non-convergence in operator norm
nodes.statement: \textbf{Remark:} $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} E(\omega_n)$ does not converge in the norm topology of $\mathcal{B}(H)$.

nodes.name: Countable additivity of $\omega \mapsto E(\omega)x$
nodes.statement: Let $x \in H$ and $\{\omega_j\}$ be a countable family of mutually disjoint Borel sets. Then $E(\bigcup_j \omega_j)x = \sum_j E(\omega_j)x$, where the right-hand side converges in the norm topology of $H$.
assumptions: $\{\omega_j\}$ be a countable family of mutually disjoint Borel sets
conclusions: $E(\bigcup_j \omega_j)x = \sum_j E(\omega_j)x$, where the right-hand side converges in the norm topology of $H$.
nodes.statement_short: For fixed $x$, $E(\cdot)x$ is countably additive with norm-convergent series.
nodes.label: lem:resId_iSum

nodes.name: Proof of countable additivity of $E(\cdot)x$
nodes.statement: Since \( E(\omega_n)E(\omega_m) = 0 \) when \( n \neq m \), the vectors \( E(\omega_n)x \) and \( E(\omega_m)x \) are orthogonal to each other (Theorem 12.14). By (\ref{itm:Re}), \begin{equation} \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} (E(\omega_n)x, y) = (E(\omega)x, y) \end{equation} for every \( y \in H \). It now follows from Theorem \ref{lem:sum_orthogonal} that: \[ \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} E(\omega_n)x = E(\omega)x. \] The series (\eqref{eq:R5}) converges in the norm topology of \( H \).
nodes.statement_short: Orthogonality of the $E(\omega_n)x$ plus weak countable additivity from (e), then the orthogonal-series criterion.

nodes.name: Weak countable additivity (R5)
nodes.statement: \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} (E(\omega_n)x, y) = (E(\omega)x, y)
nodes.label: eq:R5

nodes.name: $E(\cdot)x$ is an $H$-valued measure
nodes.statement: If \( E \) is a resolution of the identity, and if \( x \in H \), then \[ \omega \mapsto E(\omega)x \] is a countably additive \( H \)-valued measure on* \( \mathfrak{M} \).
assumptions: \( E \) is a resolution of the identity
conclusions: \[ \omega \mapsto E(\omega)x \] is a countably additive \( H \)-valued measure on* \( \mathfrak{M} \).
nodes.label: thm:resId_vectorMeasure

nodes.name: Proof of Rudin 12.18
nodes.statement: This is the summary of what is proved above.
nodes.statement_short: Summary of the preceding lemmas.

nodes.name: Countable unions of null sets are null
nodes.statement: Suppose \( E \) is a resolution of the identity. If \( \omega_n \in \mathfrak{M} \) and \( E(\omega_n) = 0 \) for \( n = 1,2,3,\dots \), and if \[ \omega = \bigcup_{n=1}^{\infty} \omega_n, \] then \( E(\omega) = 0 \).
assumptions: \( E \) is a resolution of the identity
conclusions: \( E(\omega) = 0 \)
nodes.label: thm:resId_of_zero

nodes.name: Proof of Rudin 12.19
nodes.statement: Since \( E(\omega_n) = 0 \), \( E_{x,x}(\omega_n) = 0 \) for every \( x \in H \). Since \( E_{x,x} \) is countably additive, it follows that \( E_{x,x}(\omega) = 0 \). But \[ \|E(\omega)x\|^2 = E_{x,x}(\omega). \] Hence, \( E(\omega) = 0 \).
nodes.statement_short: Pass to the countably additive positive measures $E_{x,x}$ and use $\|E(\omega)x\|^2 = E_{x,x}(\omega)$.

nodes.name: Spectrum relative to $\mathcal{B}(H)$
nodes.statement: It should perhaps be stated explicitly that the spectrum $\sigma(T)$ of an operator $T \in \mathcal{B}(H)$ will always refer to the full algebra $\mathcal{B}(H)$. In other words, $\lambda \in \sigma(T)$ if and only if $T - \lambda I$ has no inverse in $\mathcal{B}(H)$.

nodes.name: $*$-algebra
nodes.statement: Sometimes we shall also be concerned with closed subalgebras $A$ of $\mathcal{B}(H)$ which have the additional property that $I \in A$ and $T^* \in A$ whenever $T \in A$. (Such algebras are sometimes called $*$-algebras.)

nodes.name: Argument for invariance of the spectrum
nodes.statement: Let $A$ be such an algebra, and suppose that $T \in A$ and $T^{-1} \in \mathcal{B}(H)$. Since $TT^*$ is self-adjoint, $\sigma(TT^*)$ is a compact subset of the real line (Theorem 12.15), hence does not separate $\mathbb{C}$, and therefore $\sigma_A(TT^*) = \sigma(TT^*)$, by the corollary to Theorem 10.18. Since $TT^*$ is invertible in $\mathcal{B}(H)$, this equality shows that $(TT^*)^{-1} \in A$, and therefore $T^{-1} = T^(TT^*)^{-1}$ is also in $A$.
nodes.statement_short: Use that $\sigma(TT^*)$ is real so it does not separate $\mathbb{C}$, hence $(TT^*)^{-1}\in A$ and so $T^{-1}\in A$.

nodes.name: Spectrum is independent of the closed $*$-algebra
nodes.statement: Thus $T$ has the same spectrum relative to all closed *-algebras in $\mathcal{B}(H)$ that contain $T$.
conclusions: $T$ has the same spectrum relative to all closed *-algebras in $\mathcal{B}(H)$ that contain $T$

nodes.name: Spectral theorem for normal algebras of operators
nodes.statement: If $A$ is a closed normal subalgebra of $\mathcal{B}(H)$ which contains the identity operator $I$ and if $\Delta$ is the maximal ideal space of $A$, then the following assertions are true: \begin{enumerate} \item There exists a unique resolution $E$ of the identity on the Borel subsets of $\Delta$ which satisfies \begin{equation} T = \int_\Delta \widehat{T} \ dE \end{equation} for every $T \in A$, where $\widehat{T}$ is the Gelfand transform of $T$. \item The inverse of the Gelfand transform (i.e., the map that takes $\widehat{T}$ back to $T$) extends to an isometric *-isomorphism of the algebra \(L^\infty(E)\) onto a closed subalgebra $B$ of $\mathcal{B}(H)$, $B\supset A$, given by \begin{equation} \Phi f = \int_\Delta f \ dE \quad (f \in L^\infty(E)). \end{equation} Explicitly, $\Phi$ is linear and multiplicative and satisfies \[ \Phi(\bar{f}) = (\Phi f)^*, \| \Phi f \| = \| f \|_{\infty} \quad (f \in L^\infty(E)). \] \item $B$ is the closure [in the norm topology of $\mathcal{B}(H)$] of the set of all finite linear combinations of the projections $E(\omega)$. \item If $\omega \subset \Delta$ is open and nonempty, then $E(\omega) \neq 0$. \item An operator $S \in \mathcal{B}(H)$ commutes with every $T \in A$ if and only if $S$ com mutes with every projection $E(\omega)$. \end{enumerate}
assumptions: $A$ is a closed normal subalgebra of $\mathcal{B}(H)$ which contains the identity operator $I$
$\Delta$ is the maximal ideal space of $A$
conclusions: There exists a unique resolution $E$ of the identity on the Borel subsets of $\Delta$ which satisfies \begin{equation} T = \int_\Delta \widehat{T} \ dE \end{equation} for every $T \in A$, where $\widehat{T}$ is the Gelfand transform of $T$.

The inverse of the Gelfand transform (i.e., the map that takes $\widehat{T}$ back to $T$) extends to an isometric *-isomorphism of the algebra \(L^\infty(E)\) onto a closed subalgebra $B$ of $\mathcal{B}(H)$, $B\supset A$, given by \begin{equation} \Phi f = \int_\Delta f \ dE \quad (f \in L^\infty(E)). \end{equation} Explicitly, $\Phi$ is linear and multiplicative and satisfies \[ \Phi(\bar{f}) = (\Phi f)^*, \| \Phi f \| = \| f \|_{\infty} \quad (f \in L^\infty(E)). \]
$B$ is the closure [in the norm topology of $\mathcal{B}(H)$] of the set of all finite linear combinations of the projections $E(\omega)$.
If $\omega \subset \Delta$ is open and nonempty, then $E(\omega) \neq 0$.
An operator $S \in \mathcal{B}(H)$ commutes with every $T \in A$ if and only if $S$ com mutes with every projection $E(\omega)$.
nodes.statement_short: A closed normal operator algebra with identity is represented via a unique resolution of the identity on its maximal ideal space, with an isometric $L^\infty(E)$ functional calculus.
nodes.label: thm:spectralThm

nodes.name: Spectral representation $T = \int \widehat T\,dE$
nodes.statement: T = \int_\Delta \widehat{T} \ dE
nodes.label: eq:1

nodes.name: Functional calculus $\Phi f = \int f\,dE$
nodes.statement: \Phi f = \int_\Delta f \ dE \quad (f \in L^\infty(E)).
nodes.label: eq:2

nodes.name: Proof of the spectral theorem
nodes.statement: Recall that \eqref{eq:1} is an abbreviation for \begin{equation} (Tx , y) = \int_\Delta \widehat{T} \ dE_{x,y} \quad (x,y \in H, T \in A). \end{equation} Since $\mathcal{B}(H)$ is a $B^*$-algebra (Section 12.9), our given algebra $A$ is a commutative $B^*$-algebra. The Gelfand-Naimark theorem 11.18 asserts therefore that $T \to \widehat{T}$ is an isometric *-isomorphism of $A$ onto $C(\Delta)$. This leads to an easy proof of the uniqueness of $E$. Suppose $E$ satisfies \eqref{eq:4}. Since $\widehat{T}$ ranges over all of $C(\Delta)$, the assumed regularity of the complex Borel measures $E_{x,y}$ shows that each $E_{x,y}$ is uniquely determined by \eqref{eq:4}; this follows from the uniqueness assertion that is part of the Riesz representation theorem ([23], Th. 6.19) \ref{thm:ComplexRMK}. Since, by definition, $(E(\omega)x, y) = E_{x,y}(\omega)$, each projection $E(\omega))$ is also uniquely determined by \eqref{eq:4}. This uniqueness proof motivates the following proof of the existence of $E$. If $x \in H$ and $y \in H$, Theorem 11.18 shows that $ \widehat{T} \mapsto (Tx, y)$ is a bounded linear functional on $C(\Delta)$, of norm $\leq \|x\|| \|y\|$, since $\| \widehat{T}\|_{\infty} = \|T\|$. The Riesz representation theorem supplies us therefore with unique regular complex Borel measures $\mu_{x,y}$ on $\Delta$ such that \begin{equation} (Tx , y) = \int_\Delta \widehat{T} \ d\mu_{x,y} \quad (x,y \in H, T \in A). \end{equation} For fixed \( T \), the left side of \eqref{eq:5} is a bounded sesquilinear functional on \( H \), hence so is the right side, and it remains so if the continuous function \( \widehat{T} \) is replaced by an arbitrary bounded Borel function \( f \). To each such \( f \) corresponds therefore an operator \( \Phi f \in \mathcal{B}(H) \) (see Theorem 12.8) such that \begin{equation} ((\Phi f)x, y) = \int_{\Delta} f \ d\mu_{x,y} \quad (x, y \in H). \end{equation} Comparison of \eqref{eq:5} and \eqref{eq:6} shows that \( \Phi \hat{T} = T \). Thus \( \Phi \) is an extension of the inverse of the Gelfand transform. It is clear that \( \Phi \) is linear. Part of the Gelfand-Naimark theorem states that \( T \) is self-adjoint if and only if \( \hat{T} \) is real-valued. For such \( T \), \[ \int_{\Delta} \widehat{T} \ d\mu_{x,y} = (Tx, y) = (x, Ty) = \overline{(Ty, x)} = \overline{\int_{\Delta} \hat{T} d\mu_{y,x}}, \] and this implies that \( \mu_{y,x} = \overline{\mu_{x,y}} \). Hence, \[ ((\Phi \overline{f})x, y) = \int_{\Delta} \bar{f} \ d\mu_{x,y} = \overline{\int_{\Delta} f \, d\mu_{y,x}} = \overline{((\Phi f)y, x)} = (x, (\Phi f)y) \] for all \( x, y \in H \), so that \begin{equation} \Phi \bar{f} = (\Phi f)^*. \end{equation} Our next objective is the equality \begin{equation} \Phi (fg) = (\Phi f)(\Phi g) \end{equation} for bounded Borel functions \( f, g \) on \( \Delta \). If \( S \in A \) and \( T \in A \), then \( (ST)^{\wedge} = \widehat{S} \widehat{T} \); hence \[ \int_{\Delta} \hat{S} \hat{T} \ d\mu_{x,y} = (STx, y) = \int_{\Delta} \widehat{S} \ d\mu_{Tx,y}. \] This holds for every \( \widehat{S} \in C(\Delta) \); hence the two integrals are equal if \( \widehat{S} \) is replaced by any bounded Borel function \( f \). Thus \[ \int_{\Delta} f \widehat{T} d\mu_{x,y} = \int_{\Delta} f \ d\mu_{Tx,y} = ((\Phi f)Tx, y) = (Tx, z) = \int_{\Delta} \hat{T} d\mu_{x,z}, \] where we put \( z = (\Phi f)^* y \). Again, the first and last integrals remain equal if \( \widehat{T} \) is replaced by \( g \). This gives \[ \begin{aligned} (\Phi (fg)x, y) & = \int_{\Delta} fg \ d\mu_{x,y} = \int_{\Delta} g \ d\mu_{x,z} \\ & = ((\Phi g)x, z) = ((\Phi g)x, (\Phi f)^* y) = (\Phi (f) \Phi (g)x, y), \end{aligned} \] and \eqref{eq:8} is proved. We are finally ready to define \( E \): If \( \omega \) is a Borel subset of \( \Delta \), let \( \chi_{\omega} \) be its characteristic function, and put \[ E(\omega) = \Phi(\chi_{\omega}). \] By \eqref{eq:8}, \( E(\omega \cap \omega') = E(\omega)E(\omega') \). With \( \omega' = \omega \), this shows that each \( E(\omega) \) is a projection. Since \( \Phi f \) is self-adjoint when \( f \) is real, by \eqref{eq:7}, each \( E(\omega) \) is self-adjoint. It is clear that \( E(\emptyset) = \Phi(0) = 0 \). That \( E(\Delta) = I \) follows from \eqref{eq:5} and \eqref{eq:6}. The finite additivity of \( E \) is a consequence of \eqref{eq:6}, and, for all \( x, y \in H \), \[ E_{x,y}(\omega) = (E(\omega)x, y) = \int_{\Delta} \chi_{\omega} \ d\mu_{x,y} = \mu_{x,y}(\omega). \] Thus \eqref{eq:6} becomes \eqref{eq:2}. That \( \|\Phi f\| = \|f\|_{\infty} \) follows now from Theorem 12.21. This completes the proof of (\ref{itm:a}) and (\ref{itm:b}). Part (\ref{itm:c}) is now clear because every \( f \in L^{\infty}(E) \) is a uniform limit of simple functions (i.e., of functions with only finitely many values). Suppose next that \( \omega \) is open and \( E(\omega) = 0 \). If \( T \in A \) and \( \widehat{T} \) has its support in \( \omega \), \eqref{eq:1} implies that \( T = 0 \); hence \( \widehat{T} = 0 \). Since \( \widehat{A} = C(\Delta) \), Urysohn's lemma implies now that \( \omega = \emptyset \). This proves (\ref{itm:d}). To prove (\ref{itm:e}), choose \( S \in \mathcal{B}(H) \), \( x \in H \), \( y \in H \), and put \( z = S^* y \). For any \( T \in A \) and any Borel set \( \omega \subset \Delta \) we then have \begin{equation} (STx, y) = (Tx, z) = \int_{\Delta} \widehat{T} \ dE_{x,z}, \end{equation} \begin{equation} (TSx, y) = \int_{\Delta} \hat{T} \ dE_{Sx,y}, \end{equation} \[ (SE(\omega)x, y) = (E(\omega)x, z) = E_{x,z}(\omega), \] \[ (E(\omega)Sx, y) = E_{Sx,y}(\omega). \] If \( ST = TS \) for every \( T \in A \), the measures in \eqref{eq:10} and \eqref{eq:11} are equal, so that \( SE(\omega) = E(\omega)S \). The same argument establishes the converse.
nodes.statement_short: Gelfand-Naimark identifies $A$ with $C(\Delta)$; Riesz gives measures $\mu_{x,y}$ defining $\Phi$ on bounded Borel functions. The key step proves $\Phi$ multiplicative, so $E(\omega)=\Phi(\chi_\omega)$ is a resolution of the identity.

nodes.name: Weak form (4) of the spectral representation
nodes.statement: (Tx , y) = \int_\Delta \widehat{T} \ dE_{x,y} \quad (x,y \in H, T \in A).
nodes.label: eq:4

nodes.name: Riesz measures $\mu_{x,y}$ (5)
nodes.statement: (Tx , y) = \int_\Delta \widehat{T} \ d\mu_{x,y} \quad (x,y \in H, T \in A).
nodes.label: eq:5

nodes.name: Definition (6) of $\Phi f$
nodes.statement: ((\Phi f)x, y) = \int_{\Delta} f \ d\mu_{x,y} \quad (x, y \in H).
nodes.label: eq:6

nodes.name: $\Phi\bar f = (\Phi f)^*$ (7)
nodes.statement: \Phi \bar{f} = (\Phi f)^*.
nodes.label: eq:7

nodes.name: Multiplicativity (8)
nodes.statement: \Phi (fg) = (\Phi f)(\Phi g)
nodes.label: eq:8

nodes.name: Identity (10) for $STx$
nodes.statement: (STx, y) = (Tx, z) = \int_{\Delta} \widehat{T} \ dE_{x,z},
nodes.label: eq:10

nodes.name: Identity (11) for $TSx$
nodes.statement: (TSx, y) = \int_{\Delta} \hat{T} \ dE_{Sx,y},
nodes.label: eq:11

nodes.name: Approximate simple functions by Lusin
nodes.statement: Define $S$ as in Theorem 3.13. If $s \in S$ and $\varepsilon > 0$, there exists a $g \in C_c(X)$ such that $g(x) = s(x)$ except on a set of measure $< \varepsilon$, and $|g| \leq \|s\|_\infty$ (Lusin's theorem).
nodes.statement_short: Approximate each simple $s$ by $g\in C_c$ via Lusin's theorem.

nodes.name: Conclude by density of $S$
nodes.statement: Hence \begin{equation} \|g - s\|_p \leq 2\varepsilon^{1/p}\|s\|_\infty. \end{equation} Since $S$ is dense in $L^p(\mu)$, this completes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Bound $\|g-s\|_p$ and use density of simple functions.

nodes.name: Apply polar representation
nodes.statement: By Theorem \ref{thm:polar_rep}, there is a function $h$, of absolute value 1, such that $d\lambda = h \, d|\lambda|$.
nodes.statement_short: Polar representation of $\lambda$.

nodes.name: Compare densities
nodes.statement: By hypothesis, $d\lambda = g \, d\mu$. Hence \[ h \, d|\lambda| = g \, d\mu. \] This gives $d|\lambda| = \bar{h}g \, d\mu$. (Compare with Theorem 1.29.)
nodes.statement_short: Obtain $d|\lambda| = \bar h g\,d\mu$.

nodes.name: Conclude $\bar h g = |g|$
nodes.statement: Since $|\lambda| \geq 0$ and $\mu \geq 0$, it follows that $\bar{h}g \geq 0$ a.e. $[\mu]$, so that $\bar{h}g = |g|$ a.e. $[\mu]$. \qed
nodes.statement_short: Positivity forces $\bar h g = |g|$ a.e.

nodes.name: Reduce to an annihilating measure
nodes.statement: Suppose $\mu$ is a regular complex Borel measure on $X$ and $\int f \, d\mu = 0$ for all $f \in C_0(X)$.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to a measure with $\int f\,d\mu = 0$ for all $f$.

nodes.name: Polar representation
nodes.statement: By Theorem \ref{thm:polar_rep} there is a Borel function $h$, with $|h| = 1$, such that $d\mu = h \, d|\mu|$.
nodes.statement_short: Write $d\mu = h\,d|\mu|$.

nodes.name: Estimate via density
nodes.statement: For any sequence $\{f_n\}$ in $C_0(X)$ we then have \begin{equation} |\mu|(X) = \int_X (\bar{h} - f_n)h \, d|\mu| \leq \int_X |\bar{h} - f_n| \, d|\mu|, \tag{3} \end{equation} and since $C_c(X)$ is dense in $L^1(|\mu|)$ (Theorem \ref{thm:Cc_dense_Lp}), $\{f_n\}$ can be so chosen that the last expression in (3) tends to 0 as $n \to \infty$.
nodes.statement_short: Bound $|\mu|(X)$ and use density of $C_c$ in $L^1(|\mu|)$.

nodes.name: Conclude $\mu = 0$
nodes.statement: Thus $|\mu|(X) = 0$, and $\mu = 0$. It is easy to see that the difference of two regular complex Borel measures on $X$ is regular.
nodes.statement_short: Hence $\mu = 0$; differences of regular measures are regular.

nodes.name: Uniqueness
nodes.statement: This shows that at most one $\mu$ corresponds to each $\Phi$.
nodes.statement_short: Apply to the difference of two representing measures.

nodes.name: Normalize
nodes.statement: Assume $\|\Phi\| = 1$, without loss of generality.
nodes.statement_short: WLOG $\|\Phi\|=1$.

nodes.name: Reduce to constructing $\Lambda$
nodes.statement: So all depends on finding a positive linear functional $\Lambda$ that satisfies (4).
nodes.statement_short: Everything reduces to finding $\Lambda$ with (4).

nodes.name: Define $\Lambda$ on $C_c^+$
nodes.statement: If $f \in C_c^+(X)$ [the class of all nonnegative real members of $C_c(X)$], define \begin{equation} \Lambda f = \sup \{|\Phi(h)| : h \in C_c(X), |h| \leq f\}. \tag{9} \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Define $\Lambda f$ as a supremum.

nodes.name: Elementary properties
nodes.statement: Then $\Lambda f \geq 0$, $\Lambda$ satisfies (4), $0 \leq f_1 \leq f_2$ implies $\Lambda f_1 \leq \Lambda f_2$, and $\Lambda(cf) = c\Lambda f$ if $c$ is a positive constant.
nodes.statement_short: Positivity, monotonicity, homogeneity and (4).

nodes.name: Remaining tasks
nodes.statement: We have to show that \begin{equation} \Lambda(f + g) = \Lambda f + \Lambda g \quad (f \text{ and } g \in C_c^+(X)), \tag{10} \end{equation} and we then have to extend $\Lambda$ to a linear functional on $C_c(X)$.
nodes.statement_short: Need additivity (10) and an extension to $C_c(X)$.

nodes.name: Choose near-optimal $h_1, h_2$
nodes.statement: Fix $f$ and $g \in C_c^+(X)$. If $\varepsilon > 0$, there exist $h_1$ and $h_2 \in C_c(X)$ such that $|h_1| \leq f$, $|h_2| \leq g$, and \begin{equation} \Lambda f \leq |\Phi(h_1)| + \varepsilon, \quad \Lambda g \leq |\Phi(h_2)| + \varepsilon. \tag{11} \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Pick $h_i$ almost attaining $\Lambda f,\Lambda g$.

nodes.name: Superadditivity
nodes.statement: There are complex numbers $\alpha_i$, $|\alpha_i| = 1$, so that $\alpha_i \Phi(h_i) = |\Phi(h_i)|$, $i = 1, 2$. Then \begin{align} \Lambda f + \Lambda g & \leq |\Phi(h_1)| + |\Phi(h_2)| + 2\varepsilon \\ & = \Phi(\alpha_1 h_1 + \alpha_2 h_2) + 2\varepsilon \\ & \leq \Lambda(|h_1| + |h_2|) + 2\varepsilon \\ & \leq \Lambda(f + g) + 2\varepsilon, \end{align} so that the inequality $\geq$ holds in (10).
nodes.statement_short: Rotate phases to get $\Lambda f+\Lambda g \le \Lambda(f+g)$.

nodes.name: Split $h$ proportionally
nodes.statement: Next, choose $h \in C_c(X)$, subject only to the condition $|h| \leq f + g$, let $V = \{x : f(x) + g(x) > 0\}$, and define \begin{align} h_1(x) & = \frac{f(x)h(x)}{f(x) + g(x)}, \quad h_2(x) = \frac{g(x)h(x)}{f(x) + g(x)} \quad (x \in V), \tag{12} \\ h_1(x) & = h_2(x) = 0 \quad (x \notin V). \end{align} It is clear that $h_1$ is continuous at every point of $V$.
nodes.statement_short: Split $h$ into $h_1+h_2$ proportional to $f$ and $g$.

nodes.name: Continuity of $h_1, h_2$
nodes.statement: If $x_0 \notin V$, then $h(x_0) = 0$; since $h$ is continuous and since $|h_1(x)| \leq |h(x)|$ for all $x \in X$, it follows that $x_0$ is a point of continuity of $h_1$. Thus $h_1 \in C_c(X)$, and the same holds for $h_2$.
nodes.statement_short: Check $h_1,h_2\in C_c(X)$.

nodes.name: Bound $|\Phi(h)|$
nodes.statement: Since $h_1 + h_2 = h$ and $|h_1| \leq f$, $|h_2| \leq g$, we have \begin{equation} |\Phi(h)| = |\Phi(h_1) + \Phi(h_2)| \leq |\Phi(h_1)| + |\Phi(h_2)| \leq \Lambda f + \Lambda g. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Triangle inequality gives $|\Phi(h)| \le \Lambda f + \Lambda g$.

nodes.name: Subadditivity, hence (10)
nodes.statement: Hence $\Lambda(f + g) \leq \Lambda f + \Lambda g$, and we have proved (10).
nodes.statement_short: Take the sup over $h$; additivity (10) follows.

nodes.name: Extend to real and complex $f$
nodes.statement: If $f$ is now a real function, $f \in C_c(X)$, then $2f^+ = |f| + f$, so that $f^+ \in C_c^+(X)$; likewise, $f^- \in C_c^+(X)$; and since $f = f^+ - f^-$, it is natural to define \begin{equation} \Lambda f = \Lambda f^+ - \Lambda f^- \quad (f \in C_c(X), f \text{ real}) \tag{13} \end{equation} and \begin{equation} \Lambda(u + iv) = \Lambda u + i\Lambda v. \tag{14} \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Extend via $f = f^+ - f^-$ and $u + iv$.

nodes.name: Linearity of the extension
nodes.statement: Simple algebraic manipulations, just like those which occur in the proof of Theorem 1.32, show now that our extended functional $\Lambda$ is linear on $C_c(X)$.
nodes.statement_short: Routine algebra shows linearity.

nodes.name: Measure from $\Lambda$
nodes.statement: Once we have the $\Lambda$ from Lemma~\ref{lem:exists_pos_lin_func}, we associate with it a positive Borel measure $\lambda$, as in Theorem 2.14.
nodes.statement_short: Associate a positive Borel measure $\lambda$ to $\Lambda$.

nodes.name: Regularity of $\lambda$
nodes.statement: The conclusion of Theorem 2.14 shows that $\lambda$ is regular if $\lambda(X) < \infty$.
nodes.statement_short: $\lambda$ is regular when finite.

nodes.name: Bound $\lambda(X) \le 1$
nodes.statement: Since \begin{equation} \lambda(X) = \sup \{\Lambda f : 0 \leq f \leq 1, f \in C_c(X)\} \end{equation} and since $|\Lambda f| \leq 1$ if $\|f\| \leq 1$, we see that actually $\lambda(X) \leq 1$.
nodes.statement_short: Show $\lambda(X)\le 1$.

nodes.name: $L^1(\lambda)$ bound on $\Phi$
nodes.statement: We also deduce from (4) that \begin{equation} |\Phi(f)| \leq \Lambda(|f|) = \int_X |f| \, d\lambda = \|f\|_1 \quad (f \in C_c(X)). \tag{5} \end{equation} The last norm refers to the space $L^1(\lambda)$. Thus $\Phi$ is a linear functional on $C_c(X)$ of norm at most 1, with respect to the $L^1(\lambda)$-norm on $C_c(X)$.
nodes.statement_short: $\Phi$ has norm at most 1 for the $L^1(\lambda)$ norm.

nodes.name: Apply duality
nodes.statement: There is a norm-preserving extension of $\Phi$ to a linear functional on $L^1(\lambda)$, and therefore Theorem \ref{thm:Lp_duality} (the case $p = 1$) gives a Borel function $g$, with $|g| \leq 1$, such that \begin{equation} \Phi(f) = \int_X fg \, d\lambda \quad (f \in C_c(X)). \tag{6} \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Hahn-Banach extension and $L^1$ duality give $g$.

nodes.name: Extend by density
nodes.statement: Each side of (6) is a continuous functional on $C_0(X)$, and $C_c(X)$ is dense in $C_0(X)$. Hence (6) holds for all $f \in C_0(X)$, and we obtain the representation (1) with $d\mu = g \, d\lambda$.
nodes.statement_short: Density of $C_c$ in $C_0$ gives (1) with $d\mu = g\,d\lambda$.

nodes.name: Lower bound from (6)
nodes.statement: Since $\|\Phi\| = 1$, (6) shows that \begin{equation} \int_X |g| \, d\lambda \geq \sup \{|\Phi(f)| : f \in C_0(X), \|f\| \leq 1\} = 1. \tag{7} \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Obtain $\int|g|\,d\lambda \ge 1$.

nodes.name: Force equality
nodes.statement: We also know that $\lambda(X) \leq 1$ and $|g| \leq 1$. These facts are compatible only if $\lambda(X) = 1$ and $|g| = 1$ a.e. $[\lambda]$.
nodes.statement_short: Compatibility forces $\lambda(X)=1$, $|g|=1$ a.e.

nodes.name: Conclude the norm identity
nodes.statement: Thus $d|\mu| = |g| \, d\lambda = d\lambda$, by Theorem \ref{thm:abs_integral}, and \begin{equation} |\mu|(X) = \lambda(X) = 1 = \|\Phi\|, \tag{8} \end{equation} which proves (2).
nodes.statement_short: Use Rudin 6.13 to get $|\mu|(X)=\|\Phi\|$.

nodes.name: $p$ is a projection
nodes.statement: By $p = p^2$, it is a projection.
nodes.statement_short: Idempotence makes $p$ a projection.

nodes.name: Decompose via image of $p$
nodes.statement: Let $K$ be the image of $p$. Note that $x = (p + (1-p))x = px + (1-p)x$ for any $x \in H$ and $\langle px, (1-p)x\rangle = \langle x, (p-p)x\rangle = 0$.
nodes.statement_short: Take $K = \mathrm{im}\,p$ and split $x = px+(1-p)x$ orthogonally.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: So this gives the orthogonal decomposition.
nodes.statement_short: This is the orthogonal decomposition.

nodes.name: Pythagoras and Cauchy criterion
nodes.statement: Note that, by orthogonality, $\|\sum_{j=m}^n x_j\|^2 = \sum_{j=m}^n \|x_j\|^2$. Therefore, the second condition implies that the sequence $\sum_{j=1}^n x_j$ is Cauchy.
nodes.statement_short: Pythagoras makes partial sums Cauchy.

nodes.name: Converse
nodes.statement: Conversely, as $\sum_{j=1}^n x_j$ converges in norm, the square of its norm $\sum_{j=1}^n \|x_j\|^2$ converges.
nodes.statement_short: Norm convergence gives convergence of squared norms.

nodes.name: Forward direction
nodes.statement: The first condition implies the second by Cauchy-Schwartz.
nodes.statement_short: Cauchy-Schwarz.

nodes.name: Introduce $\Lambda_n$
nodes.statement: Assume that $\sum_{n=1}^\infty \langle x, y\rangle$ converges for all $y \in H$. Define $\Lambda_n y = \sum_{j=1}^n \langle y, x_j\rangle$.
nodes.statement_short: Assume weak convergence; define partial-sum functionals.

nodes.name: Uniform boundedness
nodes.statement: As this converges for each $y$, by Banach-Steinhaus, $\{\|\Lambda_n\|\}$ is bounded.
nodes.statement_short: Banach-Steinhaus bounds $\|\Lambda_n\|$.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: As $\|\Lambda_n\| = \sqrt{\sum_{j=1}^n \|x_j\|}$, this gives the first condition.
nodes.statement_short: Norms of $\Lambda_n$ give the norm criterion.

nodes.name: Orthogonality of $E(\omega_n)x$
nodes.statement: Since \( E(\omega_n)E(\omega_m) = 0 \) when \( n \neq m \), the vectors \( E(\omega_n)x \) and \( E(\omega_m)x \) are orthogonal to each other (Theorem 12.14).
nodes.statement_short: Vectors $E(\omega_n)x$ are pairwise orthogonal.

nodes.name: Weak countable additivity
nodes.statement: By (\ref{itm:Re}), \begin{equation} \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} (E(\omega_n)x, y) = (E(\omega)x, y) \end{equation} for every \( y \in H \).
nodes.statement_short: Property (e) gives weak countable additivity.

nodes.name: Norm convergence
nodes.statement: It now follows from Theorem \ref{lem:sum_orthogonal} that: \[ \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} E(\omega_n)x = E(\omega)x. \] The series (\eqref{eq:R5}) converges in the norm topology of \( H \).
nodes.statement_short: Orthogonal-series criterion upgrades to norm convergence.

nodes.name: Null on $E_{x,x}$
nodes.statement: Since \( E(\omega_n) = 0 \), \( E_{x,x}(\omega_n) = 0 \) for every \( x \in H \).
nodes.statement_short: Each $E_{x,x}(\omega_n)=0$.

nodes.name: Countable additivity
nodes.statement: Since \( E_{x,x} \) is countably additive, it follows that \( E_{x,x}(\omega) = 0 \).
nodes.statement_short: Countable additivity gives $E_{x,x}(\omega)=0$.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: But \[ \|E(\omega)x\|^2 = E_{x,x}(\omega). \] Hence, \( E(\omega) = 0 \).
nodes.statement_short: Since $\|E(\omega)x\|^2 = E_{x,x}(\omega)$, $E(\omega)=0$.

nodes.name: Spectrum of $TT^*$
nodes.statement: Let $A$ be such an algebra, and suppose that $T \in A$ and $T^{-1} \in \mathcal{B}(H)$. Since $TT^*$ is self-adjoint, $\sigma(TT^*)$ is a compact subset of the real line (Theorem 12.15), hence does not separate $\mathbb{C}$, and therefore $\sigma_A(TT^*) = \sigma(TT^*)$, by the corollary to Theorem 10.18.
nodes.statement_short: $\sigma(TT^*)$ is real so $\sigma_A(TT^*)=\sigma(TT^*)$.

nodes.name: Inverse lies in $A$
nodes.statement: Since $TT^*$ is invertible in $\mathcal{B}(H)$, this equality shows that $(TT^*)^{-1} \in A$, and therefore $T^{-1} = T^(TT^*)^{-1}$ is also in $A$.
nodes.statement_short: Hence $T^{-1}\in A$.

nodes.name: Gelfand-Naimark setup
nodes.statement: Recall that \eqref{eq:1} is an abbreviation for \begin{equation} (Tx , y) = \int_\Delta \widehat{T} \ dE_{x,y} \quad (x,y \in H, T \in A). \end{equation} Since $\mathcal{B}(H)$ is a $B^*$-algebra (Section 12.9), our given algebra $A$ is a commutative $B^*$-algebra. The Gelfand-Naimark theorem 11.18 asserts therefore that $T \to \widehat{T}$ is an isometric *-isomorphism of $A$ onto $C(\Delta)$. This leads to an easy proof of the uniqueness of $E$.
nodes.statement_short: Recall weak form (4); Gelfand-Naimark identifies $A$ with $C(\Delta)$.

nodes.name: Uniqueness of $E_{x,y}$
nodes.statement: Suppose $E$ satisfies \eqref{eq:4}. Since $\widehat{T}$ ranges over all of $C(\Delta)$, the assumed regularity of the complex Borel measures $E_{x,y}$ shows that each $E_{x,y}$ is uniquely determined by \eqref{eq:4}; this follows from the uniqueness assertion that is part of the Riesz representation theorem ([23], Th. 6.19) \ref{thm:ComplexRMK}.
nodes.statement_short: Riesz uniqueness determines each $E_{x,y}$.

nodes.name: Uniqueness of $E$
nodes.statement: Since, by definition, $(E(\omega)x, y) = E_{x,y}(\omega)$, each projection $E(\omega))$ is also uniquely determined by \eqref{eq:4}.
nodes.statement_short: Hence each $E(\omega)$ is unique.

nodes.name: Bounded functionals on $C(\Delta)$
nodes.statement: This uniqueness proof motivates the following proof of the existence of $E$. If $x \in H$ and $y \in H$, Theorem 11.18 shows that $ \widehat{T} \mapsto (Tx, y)$ is a bounded linear functional on $C(\Delta)$, of norm $\leq \|x\|| \|y\|$, since $\| \widehat{T}\|_{\infty} = \|T\|$.
nodes.statement_short: $\widehat T \mapsto (Tx,y)$ is a bounded functional on $C(\Delta)$.

nodes.name: Riesz measures $\mu_{x,y}$
nodes.statement: The Riesz representation theorem supplies us therefore with unique regular complex Borel measures $\mu_{x,y}$ on $\Delta$ such that \begin{equation} (Tx , y) = \int_\Delta \widehat{T} \ d\mu_{x,y} \quad (x,y \in H, T \in A). \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Riesz gives measures $\mu_{x,y}$ satisfying (5).

nodes.name: Define $\Phi f$
nodes.statement: For fixed \( T \), the left side of \eqref{eq:5} is a bounded sesquilinear functional on \( H \), hence so is the right side, and it remains so if the continuous function \( \widehat{T} \) is replaced by an arbitrary bounded Borel function \( f \). To each such \( f \) corresponds therefore an operator \( \Phi f \in \mathcal{B}(H) \) (see Theorem 12.8) such that \begin{equation} ((\Phi f)x, y) = \int_{\Delta} f \ d\mu_{x,y} \quad (x, y \in H). \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Sesquilinearity defines $\Phi f\in\mathcal B(H)$ for bounded Borel $f$.

nodes.name: $\Phi$ extends the inverse Gelfand transform
nodes.statement: Comparison of \eqref{eq:5} and \eqref{eq:6} shows that \( \Phi \hat{T} = T \). Thus \( \Phi \) is an extension of the inverse of the Gelfand transform. It is clear that \( \Phi \) is linear.
nodes.statement_short: $\Phi\widehat T = T$, and $\Phi$ is linear.

nodes.name: Symmetry of $\mu_{x,y}$
nodes.statement: Part of the Gelfand-Naimark theorem states that \( T \) is self-adjoint if and only if \( \hat{T} \) is real-valued. For such \( T \), \[ \int_{\Delta} \widehat{T} \ d\mu_{x,y} = (Tx, y) = (x, Ty) = \overline{(Ty, x)} = \overline{\int_{\Delta} \hat{T} d\mu_{y,x}}, \] and this implies that \( \mu_{y,x} = \overline{\mu_{x,y}} \).
nodes.statement_short: Self-adjoint $T$ have real $\widehat T$, giving $\mu_{y,x} = \overline{\mu_{x,y}}$.

nodes.name: Adjoint identity (7)
nodes.statement: Hence, \[ ((\Phi \overline{f})x, y) = \int_{\Delta} \bar{f} \ d\mu_{x,y} = \overline{\int_{\Delta} f \, d\mu_{y,x}} = \overline{((\Phi f)y, x)} = (x, (\Phi f)y) \] for all \( x, y \in H \), so that \begin{equation} \Phi \bar{f} = (\Phi f)^*. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Derive $\Phi\bar f = (\Phi f)^*$.

nodes.name: Target: multiplicativity
nodes.statement: Our next objective is the equality \begin{equation} \Phi (fg) = (\Phi f)(\Phi g) \end{equation} for bounded Borel functions \( f, g \) on \( \Delta \).
nodes.statement_short: Next goal: $\Phi(fg) = (\Phi f)(\Phi g)$.

nodes.name: Multiplicativity on $A$
nodes.statement: If \( S \in A \) and \( T \in A \), then \( (ST)^{\wedge} = \widehat{S} \widehat{T} \); hence \[ \int_{\Delta} \hat{S} \hat{T} \ d\mu_{x,y} = (STx, y) = \int_{\Delta} \widehat{S} \ d\mu_{Tx,y}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Use $(ST)^\wedge = \widehat S\widehat T$.

nodes.name: Replace $\widehat S$ by $f$
nodes.statement: This holds for every \( \widehat{S} \in C(\Delta) \); hence the two integrals are equal if \( \widehat{S} \) is replaced by any bounded Borel function \( f \). Thus \[ \int_{\Delta} f \widehat{T} d\mu_{x,y} = \int_{\Delta} f \ d\mu_{Tx,y} = ((\Phi f)Tx, y) = (Tx, z) = \int_{\Delta} \hat{T} d\mu_{x,z}, \] where we put \( z = (\Phi f)^* y \).
nodes.statement_short: Extend from $\widehat S$ to bounded Borel $f$.

nodes.name: Replace $\widehat T$ by $g$
nodes.statement: Again, the first and last integrals remain equal if \( \widehat{T} \) is replaced by \( g \). This gives \[ \begin{aligned} (\Phi (fg)x, y) & = \int_{\Delta} fg \ d\mu_{x,y} = \int_{\Delta} g \ d\mu_{x,z} \\ & = ((\Phi g)x, z) = ((\Phi g)x, (\Phi f)^* y) = (\Phi (f) \Phi (g)x, y), \end{aligned} \] and \eqref{eq:8} is proved.
nodes.statement_short: Extend to $g$ and conclude (8).

nodes.name: Define $E$
nodes.statement: We are finally ready to define \( E \): If \( \omega \) is a Borel subset of \( \Delta \), let \( \chi_{\omega} \) be its characteristic function, and put \[ E(\omega) = \Phi(\chi_{\omega}). \]
nodes.statement_short: Set $E(\omega) = \Phi(\chi_\omega)$.

nodes.name: $E(\omega)$ self-adjoint projections
nodes.statement: By \eqref{eq:8}, \( E(\omega \cap \omega') = E(\omega)E(\omega') \). With \( \omega' = \omega \), this shows that each \( E(\omega) \) is a projection. Since \( \Phi f \) is self-adjoint when \( f \) is real, by \eqref{eq:7}, each \( E(\omega) \) is self-adjoint. It is clear that \( E(\emptyset) = \Phi(0) = 0 \).
nodes.statement_short: Multiplicativity and (7) give self-adjoint projections; $E(\emptyset)=0$.

nodes.name: Remaining properties of $E$
nodes.statement: That \( E(\Delta) = I \) follows from \eqref{eq:5} and \eqref{eq:6}. The finite additivity of \( E \) is a consequence of \eqref{eq:6}, and, for all \( x, y \in H \), \[ E_{x,y}(\omega) = (E(\omega)x, y) = \int_{\Delta} \chi_{\omega} \ d\mu_{x,y} = \mu_{x,y}(\omega). \] Thus \eqref{eq:6} becomes \eqref{eq:2}.
nodes.statement_short: $E(\Delta)=I$, finite additivity and $E_{x,y} = \mu_{x,y}$.

nodes.name: Isometry
nodes.statement: That \( \|\Phi f\| = \|f\|_{\infty} \) follows now from Theorem 12.21. This completes the proof of (\ref{itm:a}) and (\ref{itm:b}).
nodes.statement_short: Isometry from Rudin 12.21; (a) and (b) done.

nodes.name: Part (c)
nodes.statement: Part (\ref{itm:c}) is now clear because every \( f \in L^{\infty}(E) \) is a uniform limit of simple functions (i.e., of functions with only finitely many values).
nodes.statement_short: Uniform approximation by simple functions.

nodes.name: Part (d)
nodes.statement: Suppose next that \( \omega \) is open and \( E(\omega) = 0 \). If \( T \in A \) and \( \widehat{T} \) has its support in \( \omega \), \eqref{eq:1} implies that \( T = 0 \); hence \( \widehat{T} = 0 \). Since \( \widehat{A} = C(\Delta) \), Urysohn's lemma implies now that \( \omega = \emptyset \). This proves (\ref{itm:d}).
nodes.statement_short: Urysohn's lemma shows an open $E$-null set is empty.

nodes.name: Part (e): setup
nodes.statement: To prove (\ref{itm:e}), choose \( S \in \mathcal{B}(H) \), \( x \in H \), \( y \in H \), and put \( z = S^* y \). For any \( T \in A \) and any Borel set \( \omega \subset \Delta \) we then have \begin{equation} (STx, y) = (Tx, z) = \int_{\Delta} \widehat{T} \ dE_{x,z}, \end{equation} \begin{equation} (TSx, y) = \int_{\Delta} \hat{T} \ dE_{Sx,y}, \end{equation} \[ (SE(\omega)x, y) = (E(\omega)x, z) = E_{x,z}(\omega), \] \[ (E(\omega)Sx, y) = E_{Sx,y}(\omega). \]
nodes.statement_short: Express $STx$, $TSx$, $SE(\omega)x$, $E(\omega)Sx$ via measures.

nodes.name: Part (e): conclude
nodes.statement: If \( ST = TS \) for every \( T \in A \), the measures in \eqref{eq:10} and \eqref{eq:11} are equal, so that \( SE(\omega) = E(\omega)S \). The same argument establishes the converse.
nodes.statement_short: Equal measures give $SE(\omega) = E(\omega)S$, and conversely.
